title: What is art? Tolstoy’s criteria

paragraphs.text: Widely criticized since its first appearance in 1898, Tolstoy’s article What is Art? is of interest not so much for the author’s own definitions of art as for his fundamental approach. His question is an old one, and has given rise to whole theories of aesthetics. He spent a lifetime trying to determine what art should be, and indeed wrote other articles on the subject. But the strength and originality of What is Art? — for all its undoubted prejudice and exaggeration — lie precisely in Tolstoy's attempt to cut through differing views to ask the questions: why do we put such an effort into the production of art, is it worth it, and what should art be? We may not agree with his conclusions, which at times are dubious, if not preposterous, but his overall handling of the problem at least provides a framework which allows us to make some kind of judgment.

Tolstoy wants to define art anew, prescribing what it should be rather than describing what it is. ‘Instead of giving a definition of true art and then deciding what is and what is not good art by judging whether a work conforms to the definition,’ he complains that ‘a certain class of works is accepted as being art, and a definition of art is then devised to cover all these productions.’

Tolstoy seems to believe that art is created spontaneously, rejecting any artistic training beyond elementary school. ‘The art of the future,’ he writes, ‘will be produced by all the members of the community who feel need of such activity, but they will occupy themselves with art only when they feel such need.’ In other words, art is a matter for amateurs, not professionals — and indeed, for Tolstoy, professionalism in art leads to the production of ‘counterfeit’ art. ‘In showing such contempt for “lessons” and “rehearsals’, then,’ Professor Caryl Emerson, of Princeton University, USA, validly asks, ‘did Tolstoy have in mind only the fabulous, the instantly gifted, for whom no sustained practice or perfected technique is required to find exquisitely correct expression?’ Moreover, Tolstoy fails to distinguish individual creativity from consciousness of artistic purpose.

What, then, is art; what is literature? Should they be something exclusive, satisfying the creator and a small group of people of similar minds? Something that satisfies the literary and artistic theorists? Or entertainment, fun? Dictionary definitions tend to be unhelpful, stressing largely formal excellence. We are, of course, talking of quality, but what kind of quality? What is ‘great’ art as opposed to that which is not so great?

Let us recall the essentials of Tolstoy’s argument. He begins by dismissing prevailing ideas about what art is: beauty, entertainment, and pleasure. These, he maintains, appeal to an aristocracy which, out of touch with ‘real’ life, has perverted art to its own purposes, leading to the production of a ‘counterfeit art’. At various points he discusses a number of artists usually considered great, maintaining that with the rare exception what they produce is either bad art or not art at all. It is here that most of us would disagree with Tolstoy, who seems almost willfully blind to the universal appeal that many such works have.

Tolstoy goes into particular detail in his discussion of ‘counterfeit art’, specifically listing four methods for producing it: (1) ‘borrowing’, by which he means borrowing a subject, usually considered poetic, from other writers; (2) ‘imitation’, by which he means imitating not other writers but life itself. He notes: ‘To value a work by the degree of accuracy with which the details are reproduced, to depict things exactly as they appear in the world, is as strange as to judge of the nutritive quality of food by its external appearance’; (3) ‘striking’, by which he means producing effects. ‘In all arts these effects consist chiefly of contrasts: in bringing together the terrible and the tender, the beautiful and the hideous, the loud and the soft, darkness and light, the most ordinary and the most extraordinary’; and (4) making something ‘interesting’, which means engaging the interest and curiosity of an audience rather than its emotions.

Tolstoy's thesis relies on the fact that art is, above all, transmission of feeling. From this it follows that art ‘is a means of union among men, joining them in the same feelings, and indispensable for the life and progress toward the well-being of individuals and of humanity.’

For Tolstoy communication with an audience is essential. Implicit in his argument is the belief that, in a general sense, art does have something to say. As Professor Rimvydas Silbajoris, of Ohio State University, USA, puts it, ‘Art is not something that is but something that happens between the artist and his audience,’ and the artist's personality appears ‘as a medium, a level of existence called consciousness, which transmits a larger truth.’

For all that Tolstoy has been criticized for his views on art, there remains in them a measure of appropriateness even when we may not agree with the specifics; he is still helpful in enabling us to assess what we personally would deem art to be. The borderline between art and non-art is narrow. It makes sense, in fact, to see art as a continuum, from the very worst non-art to the very best, the ‘great art’ to which only few aspire. In other words, rather than treating the question as an either/or proposition, trying to determine what is art and what is not, it may be more profitable to establish to what extent a given work approaches an ideal.
